scenario_stem:
Northgate Fashion Stores is a retail clothing chain operating 5 stores across a regional shopping district, employing 26 full-time sales assistants and 4 store managers. Annual revenue stands at $3.1m, and assistants are paid a time-rate wage of $13 per hour. Last year staff turnover among assistants reached 28%, and customer feedback cited slow fitting-room service and unhelpful styling advice.

The directors are deciding between two options for next year's peak season. Option one is a 4% commission on each assistant's monthly sales, which would lift top sellers' pay by around $300 a month but cut low sellers' pay. Option two keeps the time-rate wage and adds non-financial methods: job enrichment through window-display styling, teamworking incentives, and training leading to promotion to supervisor. The board meets in 3 weeks and wants a clear recommendation.

Advantage 2: Lower fixed wage cost for weak sellers [k], as 4% commission lifts top sellers' pay by $300 a month while poor performers earn less than the $13 per hour wage [app].

Benefit 2: Better retention and a promotion pipeline [k], as job enrichment and training leading to promotion to supervisor motivate ambitious assistants [app], reducing the 28% staff turnover and its recruitment costs [an].

On the other hand, the non-financial package attacks the root causes [k]: job enrichment, teamworking incentives and training leading to promotion address the feedback about styling advice [app], building loyalty and cutting the 28% turnover [an]. Overall, Northgate should keep the time-rate wage with the non-financial package rather than introduce commission [eval], because its service and retention problems stem from low engagement rather than low pay; the package protects experienced assistants and the $3.1m revenue base more reliably than commission pressure, though a small peak-season bonus could be added later to sharpen effort [eval].

scenario_stem:

Staff turnover has reached 33% this year, and wastage of milk and pastries runs at 9% of stock purchased.

Owner Priya Nair must decide how to motivate the baristas before the festive rush. One proposal is a monthly bonus of $150 for every barista in any shop that beats $14,500 in sales while keeping wastage below 8%. The alternative is a non-financial approach: rotating baristas between counter, espresso and baking duties, fortnightly training in latte art and customer service, and a lead barista promotion after 12 months.

scenario_stem:

Proposal one introduces profit sharing: 5% of annual profit ($10,500) would be split equally among the 70 full-time staff, about $150 each. Proposal two introduces job enrichment: senior housekeepers become quality captains who inspect rooms, mentor new staff and join weekly operations briefings, supported by a $9,600 training budget for inspection skills.

scenario_stem:
Maple Grove Supermarket is an independent grocery chain operating 2 stores, employing 34 checkout cashiers and 6 shelf-stacking supervisors. Cashiers are paid a time-rate wage of $12.50 per hour and work a 38-hour week. Weekly payroll for the cashiers totals $16,150, and scan rates range from 41 items per minute at one till to 55 items per minute at another.

Owner Dale Kovac is considering replacing the time-rate with a piece rate of $1.60 per 100 items scanned, arguing it would lift productivity. Alternatively, he could keep time-rate pay and add teamworking incentives: a $200 monthly bonus for the fastest-scanning shift, plus training so cashiers can rotate between tills and the customer service desk. He wants a decision within 4 weeks.

questions.model_answer: 38 hours x $12.50 per hour = $475 per week [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of switching to a piece rate of $1.60 per 100 items scanned.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Higher scan productivity [k], as pay of $1.60 per 100 items pushes cashiers toward the 55 items per minute pace seen at the fastest till rather than 41 [app]. Advantage 2: Wages vary with output [k], so labour costs only rise when tills process more items, protecting the weekly $16,150 cashier payroll budget [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of keeping time-rate pay with teamworking incentives.

Benefit 2: Greater labour flexibility and service quality [k], as trained cashiers rotate between tills and the customer service desk [app], keeping queues short and complaints low at busy periods [an].

A piece rate of $1.60 per 100 items would speed scanning [k], rewarding pace over care and risking errors and ignored customer service desk duties [app], which could harm the 2 stores' reputations [an]. Overall, Maple Grove should keep time-rate pay with teamworking incentives [eval], because the gap between 41 and 55 items per minute shows skills can improve without piece pay, and supermarket tills need accuracy and courtesy; the $200 team bonus plus rotation suits this far better than an individual piece rate [eval].

scenario_stem:
Curl & Co Hair Studio is a unisex salon on a busy shopping street, employing 11 stylists and 2 receptionists. The salon moved to this location 2 years ago. Annual revenue is $420,000, of which retail product sales account for 15%. Stylists currently earn 6% commission on every cut, colour and treatment, averaging $1,900 a month, but takings fall to $650 in quiet months. Stylist turnover reached 27% last year.

Owner Lena Ortiz wants to raise motivation before the summer wedding season. Option one increases commission to 9% and adds a quarterly bonus of $250 for the top-selling stylist. Option two keeps 6% commission but introduces a teamworking culture: shared stylist stations, joint client consultations, weekly training in new colour techniques, and a pathway to senior stylist promotion after 18 months.

questions.model_answer: Teamworking is organising employees into groups to work cooperatively on shared tasks or goals, rather than working entirely alone [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of raising commission to 9% with the $250 quarterly bonus.

Advantage 2: Extra reward for top performers [k], as the quarterly $250 bonus singles out the top-selling stylist and pushes everyone to compete for it [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of option two for Curl & Co Hair Studio.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Better client experience and loyalty [k], as shared stylist stations and joint client consultations help the 11 stylists share ideas and solve problems together [app], encouraging repeat visits and extra retail sales [an]. Benefit 2: Lower stylist turnover [k], as weekly training in colour techniques plus promotion to senior stylist after 18 months give staff a future [app], reducing the 27% turnover rate and recruitment costs [an].

Overall, Curl & Co should choose the teamworking option rather than raise commission to 9% [eval], because low, unpredictable income and 27% turnover point to disengagement rather than weak incentives; shared stations, joint consultations, weekly training and promotion after 18 months protect loyalty and client experience while the 6% base commission keeps some link between pay and effort [eval].

scenario_stem:

Option two keeps pay unchanged but creates two senior consultant posts with opportunities for promotion, fortnightly sales and product training, and a guaranteed performance review after 6 months.

Option two keeps wages at $14 and introduces non-financial motivation: job rotation between dispensary, counter and home-delivery duties, weekly huddles of 15 minutes, and training technicians as pharmacy accuracy checkers with a pay step on qualification.
